issues.legal_issue: The acquired land had non-agricultural potential beyond the portion formally converted for non-agricultural use.
material_facts: A portion of the acquired land had been converted for use by a sugar factory, while the owners claimed that the remaining land was also used for non-agricultural purposes.
The factory project report and approved scheme showed that land was required for raw materials, buildings, a workshop, staff quarters, parking, and other factory purposes.
The State produced no evidence that the remaining land was mainly used for agriculture.
Both courts below found that the remaining land had potential for non-agricultural use.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the remaining land had non-agricultural potential was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court saw no reason to disturb concurrent factual findings supported by the factory project materials and not rebutted by evidence from the State.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.factory_plans_show_non_agricultural_use: The project materials show that the land was intended for factory-related buildings, storage, access, or other non-agricultural uses.
predicates.state_lacks_evidence_of_agricultural_use: The acquiring authority produces no evidence that the disputed land was mainly used for agriculture.
predicates.concurrent_non_agricultural_potential_fi: The courts below both find that the disputed land has potential for non-agricultural use.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns acquired land and the factory materials or absence of contrary evidence support concurrent findings of non-agricultural potential, the remaining land is recognized as having that potential.

issues.legal_issue: Comparable plot sales supported the land valuation, and the appropriate deduction for development depended on the acquisition's purpose and the development actually required.
material_facts: The High Court relied on a smaller plot sale from 1976 and applied annual increases to estimate the land's value.
A further plot sale from 1982 occurred between the taking of possession and the relevant notification, so the Court considered both sales in fixing a reasonable value.
The acquired land was taken for a dam project, for which development of the kind required for a housing layout was not necessary.
The High Court had deducted 40% for development costs.
issues.conclusion: The Court affirmed the land value of Rs.6.90 per square foot and reduced the development deduction to 20%, recalculating the land compensation accordingly.
issues.legal_principle: The general approach is to allow a one-third deduction for development, but the deduction is variable according to the land's nature and location, the area to be set apart, development expenses, and acquisition purpose. The Court relied on Major General Kapil Mehra v. Union of India, (2015) 2 SCC 262, which cited Tehsildar (LA) v. A. Mangala Gowri, (1991) 4 SCC 218; Gulzara Singh v. State of Punjab, (1993) 4 SCC 245; Santosh Kumari v. State of Haryana, (1996) 10 SCC 631; Revenue Divisional Officer and LAO v. Sk. Azam Saheb, (2009) 4 SCC 395; A.P. Housing Board v. K. Manohar Reddy, (2010) 12 SCC 707; Ashrafi v. State of Haryana, (2013) 5 SCC 527; Kashmir Singh v. State of Haryana, (2014) 2 SCC 165; Haryana State Agricultural Market Board v. Krishan Kumar, (2011) 15 SCC 297; Director, Land Acquisition v. Malla Atchinaid, (2006) 12 SCC 87; Mummidi Apparao v. Nagarjuna Fertilizers & Chemicals Ltd., (2009) 4 SCC 402; and Lal Chand v. Union of India, (2009) 15 SCC 769. Lal Chand explains that the deduction is variable and may range from 20% to 75%, with less deduction appropriate where less development is needed.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_plot_sales_support_value: Sales of comparable plots provide a basis for assessing the acquired land's market value.
predicates.acquisition_does_not_require_housing_lay: The purpose of acquisition does not require the extent of development ordinarily needed for a housing layout.

issues.definition: If comparable plot sales support the valuation and the acquisition requires less development than a housing layout, the comparable-sales value is adopted with a deduction suited to the development actually needed.

issues.legal_issue: The award for damage to civil works and the transportation of usable materials was supported by the valuation evidence.
material_facts: A valuation report assessed the civil works and foundations, including dismantling costs, damage, and transportation costs for usable materials.
The State's engineer gave a different assessment of the civil works.
The High Court assessed the dismantling and damage costs together with transportation costs, and the Supreme Court found no reason to change that assessment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's award for damage to civil works and foundations and transportation of usable materials was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the assessment based on the valuation report and the evidence considered by the courts below, finding no basis in the record to adopt a different view.

predicates.valuation_evidence_assesses_material_tra: A valuation witness assesses the cost of transporting usable materials.
predicates.no_basis_to_disturb_appellate_assessment: The record gives the reviewing court no reason to alter the lower appellate court's assessment.

issues.definition: When valuation evidence assesses civil-work damage and material transport and there is no basis to disturb the appellate assessment, that award is affirmed.

issues.legal_issue: The compensation for dismantling and reinstalling electrical installations should reflect the possibility of damage during that work.
material_facts: The Reference Court awarded an amount for dismantling and reinstalling the electrical installation.
The High Court reduced that amount by treating the issue as one of depreciated market value.
The Court found that the electrical installation could be damaged during dismantling and reinstallation.
issues.conclusion: The Reference Court's award for dismantling and reinstalling the electrical installation was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Where dismantling and reinstallation create a real possibility of damage to electrical installations, compensation for that work should not be reduced merely by applying a depreciated-market-value assessment. The Court relied on the evidence and findings of the Reference Court and the High Court; it cited no separate provision or earlier case for this issue.

predicates.dismantling_creates_risk_of_damage: The dismantling and reinstallation process creates a possibility that the electrical installation will be damaged.

issues.definition: If acquired electrical installations must be dismantled and reinstalled and that work risks damage, compensation for that work is restored.

issues.legal_issue: The depreciated market value awarded for machinery and mechanical installations was supported by the valuation evidence.
material_facts: The High Court relied on the valuation report and the valuer's evidence in assessing the depreciated market value of the machinery and mechanical installation.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court's assessment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's award for the depreciated value of the machinery and mechanical installation was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the valuation reached by the High Court on the basis of the valuation report and evidence, without citing a separate provision or earlier case for this issue.

predicates.no_reason_to_disturb_appellate_assessmen: The reviewing court finds no reason to alter the lower appellate court's assessment.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for business loss was justified despite the absence of documentary proof of the claimed profits.
material_facts: The factory was idle during the period for which business-loss compensation was claimed, and evidence showed that production had stopped earlier.
The owners produced no income statement showing that the factory was making the profits they claimed.
The courts below made concurrent findings supporting compensation for loss of business during the period between the taking of possession and payment of compensation.
issues.conclusion: The compensation awarded for loss of business was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the concurrent findings on business-loss compensation in light of the factory's inactivity and the evidence on the record, despite the absence of statements proving the claimed profits. No separate provision or earlier case was cited for this issue.
